rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 8 compounds if possible and map the overall elution window without risking truncation. This gives retention coverage and a baseline for whether later optimization should focus on window narrowing, slope, or temperature.

All peaks eluted between about 4.1 and 9.4 min in the broad scout, corresponding to roughly phi_e 0.20 to 0.45, so trim the gradient window around that region to keep every compound inside the gradient and improve selectivity where the crowded pair sits. Holding tG and T constant isolates the effect of the phi window on the unresolved 4/5 pair.

The trimmed window fully resolved all pairs, so the next move is to shorten the gradient to recover time while staying in the same selective region. This tests how much resolution margin we can give back before any pair drops below 1.5.

At 12 min the slope became too steep and two pairs collapsed, while 20 min had excess resolution but too much time penalty. An intermediate tG of 16 min should restore those slope-sensitive pairs above 1.5 while keeping t_last closer to 10 min.

The current method is fully resolved but pays a time penalty, and the closest pair still has some margin at R 1.85. Raising temperature should shorten retention and may preserve enough selectivity to keep all pairs above 1.5, improving CRF.

At 45 C the run got faster and improved CRF, but one pair slipped just below full-credit resolution; a slightly longer gradient should recover that pair with only a modest time penalty. This directly tests whether the loss at 45 C is mainly slope-driven rather than requiring a different composition window.

Because the 3/4 pair stayed at the same resolution when tG increased, it appears relatively insensitive to slope and more sensitive to the composition window. Narrowing the upper end of the window should change selectivity around the crowded middle while also pulling the late peaks earlier.

Lowering phi1 worsened run time without helping the critical 3/4 pair, so test the opposite direction and slightly widen the upper window. This may shift selectivity enough to open that pair while also shortening the late-eluting region.

Increasing phi1 to 0.50 gave a large CRF gain by shortening t_last with only a tiny loss on the same critical pair, so one more step higher is worth testing. This could bring t_last to 10 min or below while checking whether the 3/4 pair remains acceptably resolved.

The 0.20–0.50, 16 min, 45 C method is the current best, with only one slightly subcritical pair and minimal time penalty. Shortening tG by one step tests whether we can eliminate the remaining time penalty without sacrificing too much resolution on the 3/4 pair.

The best region appears to be around phi1 = 0.50 at 45 C, and the remaining issue is a mildly under-resolved early-middle pair. Lowering phi0 by one step may change selectivity for that pair without pushing the late peaks past 10 min because the current method is already near the time limit.

Lowering phi0 hurt both selectivity and time, so test the opposite direction around the current best window. Raising phi0 may shift the critical 3/4 pair's selectivity while compressing the run slightly, potentially improving on the 0.20–0.50 method.

The best method is already near the 10 min target and appears limited by one selectivity-sensitive pair, so temperature is the remaining strong lever. Testing 50 C checks whether a modest thermal selectivity shift can improve that pair enough to offset the shorter retention, while keeping run time very favorable.

Since raising temperature to 50 C catastrophically collapsed the critical pair, the selectivity optimum is likely on the lower-temperature side of 45 C. Testing 35 C checks whether that pair opens enough to outweigh the added retention time and potentially beat the current best.

At 40 C with the narrower 0.20–0.45 window, all pairs were resolved but the run was too long; with phi1 increased to 0.50 the late peaks should come earlier while 40 C may improve the temperature-sensitive critical pair relative to 45 C. This targets a possible sweet spot between the strong selectivity of 40 C and the favorable timing of the 0.50 upper bound.

At 40 C and phi1 = 0.50, the 18 min run nearly achieved full credit but paid mainly in time, so a shorter gradient may keep both critical pairs near or above the threshold while pulling t_last toward 10 min. This is a focused test of whether 40 C can outperform the current best when the slope is made more aggressive.

We have not yet tested the best composition window at 45 C with a slightly longer gradient than the current best. Since 16→18 min at phi1 = 0.45 did not help the critical pair, this run checks whether at phi1 = 0.50 the extra slope margin specifically improves the emerging 6/7 pair enough to raise total resolution credit.

The main remaining opportunity is to balance the excellent time of higher phi1 against the slight resolution losses around the two critical pairs. Testing phi1 = 0.55 with a shorter gradient maps whether that region can preserve the better 3/4 behavior seen at 0.50 while keeping t_last comfortably under 10 min.

The best two runs are clustered at phi0 0.20, phi1 0.50, T 45, with 14–16 min both strong; testing 12 min completes the local slope map at the current best composition window. If resolution holds up, it could remove the remaining time penalty and surpass the current best, while if not it confirms 16 min is near-optimal.

The data suggest 40 C helps the late critical pair while higher phi1 controls run time, so combining those two levers is the most promising unexplored region. This run tests whether phi1 = 0.55 can offset the longer retention at 40 C while preserving or improving the stronger pairwise resolution seen at lower temperature.

Most useful composition and slope combinations have now been mapped, and the unresolved behavior appears strongly temperature-selective, so one extreme-temperature probe is worth spending to rule in or out a beneficial order change. If 60 C reshuffles the critical pair favorably it could unlock a shorter fully efficient method; if not, it confirms 45 C as the practical optimum.

With only a few shots left, the strongest unexplored direction near the current optimum is one more increase in phi1 at the otherwise best settings. This tests whether there is a narrow gain in time around a still-acceptable selectivity window, or whether 0.50 is indeed the optimum upper bound.

Most winning regions cluster near 40–45 C and phi1 0.45–0.50, and we have not tested the potentially favorable combination of the strong 40 C selectivity with a slightly higher phi0 and longer gradient in that lower-phi1 window. This is a last focused attempt to separate the late critical pair that improved at 40 C while keeping the gradient shallow enough to protect both difficult regions.

With only two runs left, the best untested neighbor around the fully resolved 40 C method is a slightly lower phi0 while keeping the gentler 0.45 upper bound and 16 min slope. This probes whether the strong 40 C selectivity can be retained while shifting the early-middle critical region away from the collapse seen at higher phi0 and higher phi1.

The remaining untested nearest neighbor to the campaign optimum is a slightly longer gradient at the same best composition window and temperature. This is the last chance to see whether the stubborn 3/4 pair can gain enough resolution credit at 45 C to outweigh the modest extra time penalty.
